fderoles.q: Which role usually builds and ships the production deployment inside the customer's environment?
options: Sales Engineer
Forward Deployed Engineer
Customer Success Manager
Account Executive
fderoles.why: The FDE owns the working build through go-live. The SE supports the sale, the CSM owns the relationship after go-live and the AE owns the deal.

fderoles.q: Roughly what share of an FDE's time does the course material say goes to code and model work?
options: 10 to 20 percent
30 to 40 percent
70 to 80 percent
Close to 100 percent
fderoles.why: Around 70 to 80 percent. The rest goes to discovery, demos and writing, which still matter; it is never close to 100 percent.

fderoles.q: You join a deal the day after contract signature. What do you ask the sales engineer for first?
options: Their commission plan, so you know their incentives
The product roadmap for next year
A handoff: promises, success criteria, demo data, people and risks
A new demo to show the customer again
fderoles.why: Most trouble starts with promises and risks lost at the handoff. Getting them in writing lets you confirm scope with the customer early.

fderoles.q: A posting titled 'Solutions Architect' says 'build and deploy production integrations, write Python daily'. What is it closest to?
options: An FDE-style build role
A pure pre-sales demo role
A customer success role
An account executive role
fderoles.why: Judge a job by its verbs. Building and deploying production code daily is FDE-like work, whatever the title says.

fderoles.q: Spot the mistake: an FDE says 'I did 12 demos this month, so my build share is fine.' What is wrong with that thinking?
options: Demos are always the most valuable part of the job
Demos are not build work; logging the week would show if code time fell
Twelve demos is too few for an FDE
Build share only matters in the first week
fderoles.why: Demos are customer contact, not code and model work. Measuring the week shows whether build time has drifted below the target.

fdeskills.q: Which list names the five axes of the FDE skills radar used in this lesson?
options: Speed, accuracy, cost, security, scale
Technical depth, problem finding, customer empathy, product judgment, ownership
Python, SQL, cloud, LLMs, Docker
Sales, marketing, support, finance, legal
fdeskills.why: The radar covers the whole job: building, finding the real problem, understanding people, deciding what to build and owning the result. Tool lists are part of technical depth only.

fdeskills.q: What does 'T-shaped' mean for an FDE?
options: Expert in every area of the stack
Deep in one area and unaware of the rest
Able to work both on site and remote
Working breadth across many areas plus one deep spike
fdeskills.why: The top bar is breadth, the stroke is one deep specialty. Nobody is expert in everything, and a spike with no breadth fails on site.

fdeskills.q: You rate yourself 4 on problem finding but cannot name one project where you found the real need. What should you do?
options: Cap it at 2 and plan work that creates evidence
Keep the 4 because you feel confident
Drop the axis because it is not technical
Ask the interviewer to skip that round
fdeskills.why: Without evidence the score is a guess. Capping it and planning an output, such as leading a discovery session, makes the rating honest and gives you a next step.

fdeskills.q: A client says 'use AI to make claims faster' and nothing more. What shows comfort with ambiguity?
options: Wait until they send a full specification
Build a chatbot at once and hope it helps
List assumptions, test the riskiest cheaply, then decide and write it down
Tell them the request is too vague to work on
fdeskills.why: You make progress without pretending to be certain: separate facts from guesses and test the guess that would change the plan most.

fdeskills.q: Spot the trap: 'My technical score is 5, so the other axes do not matter for an FDE role.' What is wrong?
options: Nothing, code is all the interview checks
FDE interviews and projects test all five axes, and low people skills fail engagements
A 5 is impossible, so the score is wrong
Technical depth is not part of the radar
fdeskills.why: FDE loops have customer and business rounds, and real engagements fail when the builder misses the real problem or the people. Balance matters more than one peak.

asyncwriting.q: What does BLUF mean for a work message?
options: Background, links, updates, follow-up
A polite opening before any request
The first line states the point or the request
Sending the message to the whole team at once
asyncwriting.why: Bottom line up front: readers decide from the first line, so the point or ask goes there. Background comes after it.

asyncwriting.q: Which three details make a request easy to act on?
options: A named owner, a deadline and a clear question
A greeting, an apology and a thank-you
A long history, a link and a screenshot
Tagging everyone, bold text and a reminder
asyncwriting.why: One owner knows it is theirs, the deadline says when, and a clear question can be answered quickly. Extra people and history slow it down.

asyncwriting.q: You finish at 17:00 in Toronto and the customer starts at 9:00 in Singapore. What is the best way to keep work moving?
options: Stay online until midnight to answer questions
Wait for the weekly status call
Email the customer's CEO a summary each night
Post an end-of-day note with done, next, blocked and named needs
asyncwriting.why: With no overlap, the written EOD note is the handoff. The customer can act on your needs in their morning, and you find answers when you start.

asyncwriting.q: A debugging thread in the shared customer channel needs the database connection string. What do you do?
options: Paste it and delete it after they copy it
Share it through the approved secrets vault and reference it in the thread
Post it in a direct message to the engineer
Put it in the ticket description instead
asyncwriting.why: Secrets never go in chat or tickets, even briefly, because messages are stored and notifications are sent. Use the vault and point to it.

asyncwriting.q: Spot the mistake: 'Hi all, quick update on a few things from this week...' is followed by 4 paragraphs, with the ask in the last line. What is wrong?
options: It should open with a joke to keep attention
Updates should never be written down
The ask is buried, so readers may miss it or act late
It needs more background before the ask
asyncwriting.why: Readers skim the first line. The ask with its owner and date should come first, with the context underneath.

options: A law that stops companies sharing any data
A rule that lets you share customer data after one year
A contract defining what information is confidential and how it may be used
A document listing the customer's approved AI tools
ethics.why: An NDA is a contract between parties about confidential information. It is not a general law, and it does not list tools.

ethics.q: Which statement about a model's accuracy is the most honest?
options: It is 97 percent accurate on 500 typed invoices; scans are around 90 percent
It is 97 percent accurate
It is nearly perfect in our demos
It will reach 100 percent once it learns from you
ethics.why: An honest number states the conditions and the weak spots. Bare or demo-based figures mislead, and 'it will learn' may not be true.

ethics.q: You want to test a prompt on 20 real customer records tonight. What should you do?
options: Use a masked sample in the customer-approved environment
Email them to your personal account to work from home
Ask a friend at another company to try them
Paste them into a free AI chat app, then delete the chat
ethics.why: Only approved tools covered by the data agreement, with the minimum masked data. Deleting a chat afterwards does not undo sharing.

ethics.q: A customer offers you expensive concert tickets at year-end. What is the right first step?
options: Check your company's gift policy, then decline or declare as it requires
Accept, since customers expect it
Accept and give them to a colleague
Accept only if the project is finished
ethics.why: Gift rules are written in your code of conduct and often require declaring or declining anything above a small value.

ethics.q: Spot the mistake: 'Bank B asked what other banks do about fraud, so I showed them Bank A's new scoring rules.' What went wrong?
options: Nothing, since both are customers
Confidential information from one customer was shared with another
The FDE should have charged for the advice
The rules should have been emailed instead
ethics.why: Information from one customer never goes to another. You can share general public patterns and your own product's capabilities.
